question.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{′}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u={x}^{2}+2x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (2x+2) \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+2x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}+2\cdot 0-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $2\operatorname{cos}⁡1.$
